Daniel, welcome back! How was the trade fair in Sao Paulo?
Busy, but very good. We had a booth near the entrance, so hundreds of people walked past us every day.
That sounds great. Did you meet anyone interesting?
Yes. On the second day, I was setting up the screen when a buyer from a big supermarket chain stopped at the booth.
Really? What did you do?
I pitched our food program right there, in ten minutes. She loved it. Now she is one of our best leads.
Fantastic. And how was the trip? Did you have jet lag?
Not really, the time difference is small. But on the last night I was so tired that I fell asleep during the dinner!
How was your trip?
It was snowing when we arrived in Toronto.
We came back with more than twenty good leads.
What brought you to this event?

Last year I organized a trade mission to Toronto. We had a delegation of twelve Brazilian companies, mostly from the food and technology sectors. When we arrived at the airport, it was snowing, and all the flights were late. Some of the companies were seeing snow for the first time, so everybody was taking photos. On the first day, we visited a trade fair, and in the evening we had a dinner with Canadian partners. That dinner was the best moment of the trip. People were talking, exchanging business cards, and making plans. In the end, the companies came back with more than forty leads.

I remember my first pitch in Canada very well. I was presenting my products to a group of six buyers, and I was a little nervous. While I was talking about our prices, the projector stopped working. The room was quiet, and everybody was looking at me. For a second I did not know what to do. Then I closed my laptop and continued without slides. I told the story of my company, how my father started it, and why our products are different. When I finished, one of the buyers said: that was the best part of the presentation. Today, that buyer is our biggest client in Canada.

Here is something I learned after twenty years of conferences. Most partnerships do not start during the talks. They start during the coffee breaks and the dinners, when people are relaxing. So when you go to an event, do not stay in your seat. Go and network. My favorite question to start a conversation is simple: what brought you to this event? And when people ask about you, tell a short story, not only your job title. Something that happened to you, something you learned. People remember stories. A week later, they do not remember your job title, but they remember the story you told.
